dialogue.text: I'm Mizuki, thirty-three. Last week I registered for the bookkeeping certification, level three to begin with, which means opening a textbook for the first time since my junior college diploma.
Twelve years away from studying and you've booked yourself an exam date. What decided it?
A permanent girl in accounts asked me to check her figures because I am faster than she is. She is twenty-six and earns more than me for the same desk.
So the certificate isn't really about the arithmetic. It's about having something on paper that the desk arrangement can't argue with.

sessions.summary: Mizuki, thirty-three, registers for a bookkeeping certification twelve years after her last studying, prompted by checking the figures of a better-paid younger colleague.

dialogue.text: I do the office administration at a machinery trading company on a one-year renewable contract, and I am the only woman in the section who is not permanent. Every March I find out in a two-line email whether I still have work in April.
A whole year of your life renewed in two lines. That arrangement makes it hard to plan anything at all.
One thing has already helped. I started arriving twenty minutes before Hasegawa instead of exactly on time, and the pile of urgent things waiting on my desk stopped being a surprise.
You bought yourself the first look at the day. Twenty minutes of knowing beats an hour of reacting.

sessions.summary: On a one-year renewable contract and the only non-permanent woman in her section, Mizuki starts arriving before her senior colleague and stops being ambushed by her own desk.

dialogue.text: I'm Japanese and I still live in my mother's house in Nagoya, which at my age is a sentence I hate saying out loud. Sunday lunch has one subject and it is not the certification.
One subject, once a week, for years. Even a gentle version of that becomes a weather system.
She has lived in that house since she married in 1986 and has never spent a single night anywhere else. To her, leaving a house is something that happens to you, not something you decide.
Then your moving out isn't only about rent to her. It's a different theory of how lives are supposed to work.

Being wrong twice is apparently the price of it sticking. That's an inconvenient discovery but a usable one.
It makes me feel stupid though. The others in the cram school seem to read something once and own it.
You are watching their results and comparing them to your process. Nobody's second wrong answer happens in public.

dialogue.text: I submitted the conversion application in June through Ms Sanada, and there has been no acknowledgement of any kind since.
Not even a receipt. Applications that vanish are harder to live with than applications that are refused.
I cannot ask twice. Asking twice about your own status here is read as a complaint, and complaints attach to the person who makes them.
So the one lever available to you carries a cost that lands on you rather than on the delay. That's a closed loop.

A whole afternoon in her territory, on her expertise, with nothing to defend. That is a rare configuration in your house.
She corrected my measurements four times and enjoyed every correction. I have never seen her like that with me.
Being the one who knows suits her. And for once being corrected cost you nothing at all.

I told nobody at work. It felt like something that would be used against me if the wrong person heard it.
Then it stays yours until it's useful. There will be a moment when saying it costs less than it does now.

Knowing the odds doesn't change your application, but it does change what the waiting means. Fewer stories to invent about why.

So there is a door as well as a plan. Naming the door usually makes the waiting more bearable, not less.

Mr Fujii at the cram school went through it with me and did not soften anything. He said I lose the marks in the same place every time, on the consolidated entries.

I thanked him. On the way back to my desk I realised I had thanked him for nothing at all.
The thanking is automatic in that room. Noticing it afterwards is the part that matters.

dialogue.text: I have started separating the two things I have been calling nerves: the flat dread before a status meeting, and the sharp kind before an exam. The exam one burns off by the second question; the meeting one never does.
What I took: one is anticipation that a task can discharge, and the other has no task at the end of it to discharge into.
That is exactly it. In an exam there is something to do with my hands. In the meeting room I just sit there and get looked at.
So the fear that has work attached is survivable, and the fear that only has waiting attached isn't. Useful thing to know about yourself.

dialogue.text: I asked Sae for her number instead of waiting to be asked, and the class has turned into something that continues on Saturdays.
What I took: the thing you had been treating as impossible took one sentence, and the friendship was already there waiting for it.
She said she had wanted to ask me for months and assumed I was private. We had both been waiting for the other one to go first.
Two people being careful in the same direction for months. Somebody had to spend the sentence, and it turned out to be cheap.

sessions.summary: Asking Sae for her number rather than waiting turns the pottery class into a Saturday friendship, after months of both women assuming the other preferred distance.

dialogue.text: Registration is open. It is held three times a year, but only the November sitting is at the hall in the city — the others are an hour and a half out on a Sunday morning.
What I took: November isn't only your deadline, it is also the only sitting that doesn't start with a ninety-minute journey.
So it is November or it is a much worse day. I have booked it and paid, which for me is the point of no return.
Booked and paid, in the venue that costs you the least before you even sit down. That's the version of the plan that was always going to work.

sessions.summary: Only the November sitting is held at the city hall rather than ninety minutes away, so Mizuki books and pays for it as her point of no return.

dialogue.text: Another meeting about my status. Forty minutes, three people, and nothing on paper at the end of it.
What I took: the meeting existed so that a meeting could be said to have happened. You have been in this exact room before.
Meanwhile Mr Obara found me a second apartment, smaller, two minutes from the station, and I signed on the Saturday without asking anyone first.
One room where nothing can be decided, and one where you decided in an afternoon. Hard to miss which of those you control.

sessions.summary: A third status meeting produces nothing on paper, while Mizuki signs for a smaller apartment two minutes from the station without consulting anyone.

dialogue.text: Moving day was the part I had dreaded for two years. What I did differently was hand my mother the kitchen boxes to pack instead of doing every single thing myself, and Yuka worked beside her all morning. By the evening she was telling Haru next door which window my desk would face, and nobody has mentioned me coming back since.
What I took: you gave her a job inside the thing she was losing, and she made it hers. By the time she was describing it over the fence it had become her story too.
Aunt Chizuko still thinks I have abandoned the house. But my mother did not say one word of that all day, and she is the one who has the right to.
The person with the strongest claim declined to make it. That is worth more than the aunt's version, however loudly it is being told.

sessions.summary: On the dreaded moving day Mizuki hands her mother the kitchen packing; by evening her mother is describing the new flat to a neighbour and never mentions returning.

dialogue.text: First kiln day at the studio near the new place. Sae came over on the Saturday morning and we walked there together, and it was the first time anyone has ever come to a home that is mine.
What I took: not just a friend and not just an apartment, but the two of them in the same morning. Three years ago neither existed.
My bowl came out cracked across the base. I did not mind nearly as much as I expected to.
The bowl was never the point of the morning. You seem to have worked that out somewhere between the walk and the kiln.

sessions.summary: Sae visits the new apartment before the first kiln day, the first guest in a home of Mizuki's own, and a cracked bowl barely registers.

dialogue.text: The night before the sitting I did not open a single book. I walked the route to the exam hall instead, found the room number and worked out where I would buy coffee. On the day I sat down eleven minutes early without the shaking hands I had at level three.
What I took: the last night was never going to add knowledge, so you spent it removing unknowns instead. By the morning there was nothing left to be surprised by.
The consolidated entries came up as the second question. I wrote out every line of working, the way Takumi told me, and I did not look at the clock once.
The exact place you lost four marks in June, met with the exact habit you built afterwards. Whatever the result says, that part is already yours.

sessions.summary: Instead of studying, Mizuki walks the exam route the night before and arrives eleven minutes early without shaking, meeting the consolidated entries in question two.
